title: Ideation, Prototyping, and Strategic Experimentation
content:
Stepping into the fifth week of our Information Systems Honours programme, we entered what is known as Maker Week, where the focus shifted entirely from high level theoretical frameworks to the messy, unpredictable reality of ideation and prototyping. Up until this point, discussing digital strategy in a lecture theatre felt relatively controlled. However, the requirement to actually design a strategically grounded solution for our group project quickly tested our assumptions and forced us to confront the practicalities of strategic experimentation. Perhaps the most profound lesson I took away from this week was that in the realm of design thinking, failure is not a setback to be feared; rather, it is a highly effective diagnostic tool. This became glaringly obvious during our initial project phase when we attempted to focus our digital solution on local spaza shops. We had gathered our fieldwork data and confidently stood up to pitch our first empathy map to the class and the lecturer, expecting validation. Instead, the pitch completely fell apart. The empathy map was disjointed and pointed in far too many different directions. The lecturer was lost, the class was confused, and it became painfully clear that our group did not have a coherent vision of the exact problem we were trying to solve within the informal retail sector.

When we reflected on our initial research with the spaza shop owners, we realised a harsh truth: they simply did not have a specific, pressing digital problem that they actually wanted us to solve. We were falling into the trap of trying to force a technological solution onto a community that did not need it. While this public failure was a difficult pill to swallow, it perfectly illustrated the concept of failing fast, which is an essential strategic capability in agile environments. Embracing this failure allowed us to navigate our uncertainty and completely pivot our focus to a different sector where the pain points were much more visible and actionable. We redirected our energy towards the hair and beauty sector, specifically targeting students on our campus who run their own local hair salons and barbershops. This strategic pivot changed the entire trajectory of our project. Because we were dealing with a demographic that actively struggled with highly specific operational issues (such as no shows, disorganised bookings, and clashing university timetables) we were finally able to gather rich, meaningful data. It taught me that genuine innovation cannot be forced; it requires active iteration and the humility to accept when an initial idea simply does not fit reality.

However, finding the right problem was only the beginning; the actual ideation phase presented its own unique set of frustrations and breakthroughs. During our brainstorming sessions, we were instructed to engage in divergent thinking by coming up with twenty distinct ideas each. Initially, this exercise sparked a tremendous amount of creativity. It pushed us to think far outside the box to generate novel concepts for the beauty and wellness space. Yet, as we pushed past the tenth or twelfth idea, a distinct sense of repetition set in. The core problems faced by these campus barbers were fundamentally quite straightforward, meaning that our elaborate solutions soon started sounding exactly the same, just dressed up in different technological buzzwords. This repetition was incredibly frustrating at first, but it ultimately led to a vital strategic realisation. In constrained, informal environments, innovation does not necessarily mean inventing twenty wildly different technological paradigms. Often, the most effective digital strategy is a single, simple methodology that is executed flawlessly. We learned that while divergent ideation is necessary to explore the boundaries of a problem space and embrace uncertainty, the ultimate goal is to converge on a solution that is highly practical rather than overly complex.

This crucial lesson in practicality heavily influenced our decision making when it came time to select our final prototypes. As an individual who is deeply fascinated by the cutting edge of technology, the solution I was most reluctant to let go of was our concept for a virtual reality or augmented reality integration. We had brainstormed a virtual try on feature where clients could use their phone cameras to instantly visualise how different hairstyles or fades would look on them before they committed to booking. Conceptually, it is a brilliant idea that aligns perfectly with the rapid technological innovation of a modern digital society. However, strategic experimentation requires us to brutally assess economic viability and business capability. Building a functional augmented reality tool is highly resource intensive. It is simply too expensive, technically demanding, and would take far too much time for an informal campus business to realistically implement or afford. Letting go of the virtual try on feature was a humbling exercise in strategic discipline. It reinforced the reality that as an emerging Information Systems professional, I cannot let my fascination with high tech solutions override the actual feasibility of the project.

As we move into the prototyping phase, we are applying these lessons of simplicity and speed directly to our execution strategy. Instead of sinking weeks into developing a complex application from scratch, we plan to utilise quick artificial intelligence app builders or construct wireframes using dummy data at the backend. Time constraints are a very real factor, and our primary objective is not to present a finished, polished software product. Our goal is to quickly get a working concept into the hands of the barbers so we can run test runs, explain the core concepts, and observe how the users interact with the system. This approach encapsulates the very essence of prototyping as a strategic capability: we are building just enough to test our assumptions, allowing the community feedback to guide the next iteration before any significant resources are committed. Reflecting on Maker Week, my understanding of what makes a successful Information Systems strategy has deeply matured. I now view uncertainty, failure, iteration, and continuous learning not as project risks to be avoided, but as the exact strategic capabilities that drive genuine, sustainable innovation in the digital economy.
